2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern / Not applicable (cross-sectional design): There is no longitudinal follow-up, and household survey non-response is reported as very low (99.19% response rate across 120 households in Section 2.1, PDF p. 3, though 119/120 equals 99.17% and exact refusal/replacement counts are not reported).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: No statistical adjustment, stratification, or multivariable regression is conducted to account for confounders of the water-poverty relationship (such as municipal SDE pipe network reach at expanding urban boundaries, informal/unparceled land tenure, household size, or tourism-driven neighborhood heterogeneity). Inferences rely solely on visual comparison of univariate GIS maps.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Legal, regulatory, and tariff frameworks—specifically the 1995 Senegalese water sector reform (cited in the Abstract, PDF p. 1), urban encroachment of Mbour onto the rural community of Malicounda (Section 3.1, PDF p. 4), unparceled squatter settlements (Section 2, PDF p. 3), and the disparity between standpipe prices (1750 CFA francs/m3) and the SDE social tariff (191 CFA francs/m3; Section 4, PDF p. 7)—are referenced only as contextual narrative assertions without primary statutory/contractual citations or household/spatial coding of legal exposure.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Household economic status relies on undocumented questionnaire items that conflate consumption and income and apply an ad hoc 600 CFA franc poverty line (Sections 2.2 and 3.2, PDF pp. 3, 5). Daily per-capita water availability (Water Access Index) uses differential measurement modes (bi-monthly utility bills for paying households versus estimated container and tank capacities for non-paying households; Section 3.4, PDF p. 6) and benchmarks domestic water use against national total per-capita water withdrawals (0.58 m3/person/day, or 580 L/person/day). Claims of polluted well water (PDF pp. 1, 7) are unsupported by microbiological or chemical water testing.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Water access and water-poverty outcomes suffer from unvalidated survey instruments, differential measurement across billed and unbilled households, lack of physical inspection or water-quality testing, extrapolation of a single centroid household's response to an entire 500 m x 500 m (25-hectare) urban grid cell (Section 2, PDF p. 3), and miscalibrated Water Access Index cutoffs (0-0.25 m3/person/day labeled 'very low access' by misapplying national agricultural/industrial/municipal water withdrawal averages to household domestic consumption; Section 3.4, PDF p. 6).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No survey instrument or pre-analysis protocol is provided. Although Section 2 and Section 2.1 (PDF pp. 2-3) state that indicators of water quality and sanitation were established, that interviews were conducted with four institutional agencies, and that SPSS statistical processing and geostatistical autocorrelation/interpolation models were used, no sanitation data, water-quality measurements, interview analyses, correlation coefficients, confidence intervals, or spatial autocorrelation parameters are reported in Results; several key percentages are drawn from an unpublished Master's thesis (Toure, 2009).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: While a systematic 500 m spatial grid covering Mbour (120 grid cells, excluding the municipal soccer stadium) was used with a reported 99.19% response rate (Sections 2-2.1, PDF pp. 2-3), selecting only one household per 25-hectare cell near the GPS centroid without documented household/respondent eligibility rules or population-density weighting under-samples high-density poor districts relative to low-density tourist zones and introduces spatial representation bias when extending one household's attributes to the entire mesh cell.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: The spatial sampling frame is defined as a regular 500 m grid mesh laid over a Kompsat satellite image of Mbour (excluding one central cell occupied by the municipal soccer stadium), with one point placed at each cell centroid via GPS to select 120 households. However, household-level and respondent-level eligibility/inclusion criteria—such as how a single household was chosen near each centroid when multiple dwellings, compounds, or non-residential plots were present, or who within the household was eligible to respond—are not stated.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 (Materials and methods), PDF pp. 2-3, Figs. 2-3

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the geographic setting of Mbour (80 km southwest of Dakar, neighborhood layout, tourism zone around Saly, and encroachment onto rural Malicounda) is mapped and described, the surveyed sample itself is not described in detail. Exact fieldwork dates/seasons are omitted, no demographic table of surveyed households is reported, and instead of reporting actual sample household sizes, the authors extrapolate from a 2004 national survey average of 9.8 persons per household (Sylla, 2004).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1, PDF p. 1; Section 2 & Section 2.1, PDF pp. 2-3; Sections 3.1-3.2, PDF pp. 4-5

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Household poverty (the primary socioeconomic exposure examined in relation to water access) was not measured with a documented or validated survey module. The paper omits recall periods, item lists, and adult-equivalence adjustments, conflates consumption poverty in Section 2.2 ('population whose consumption is lower than this sum') with income poverty in Sections 3.2-3.3 ('income poverty affects 62%', 'monthly income'), and replaces the World Bank $1.25 (2005 PPP) benchmark with an ad hoc 600 CFA franc cutoff based on an outdated nominal $1 exchange rate.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.2, PDF p. 3; Sections 3.2-3.3, PDF pp. 5-6

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: While the Global Water Partnership affordability benchmark (>5% of monthly income spent on water) is a recognized threshold, other classifications deviate from objective standard criteria: the poverty threshold was altered ad hoc to 600 CFA francs, and the custom Water Access Index (WAI) misapplies national total renewable/withdrawal averages from ChartsBin (0.58 m3/person/day = 580 L/person/day, which includes agricultural and industrial water) to domestic household use, classifying 0-0.25 m3/person/day (up to 250 L/person/day) as 'very low access to water'.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.2, PDF p. 3; Sections 3.3-3.4, PDF p. 6

domain_ratings.justification: Potential confounders of the household poverty-water relationship—such as municipal SDE network non-coverage in newly settled boundary zones, informal/unparceled land tenure, household size, and tourism enclave development—are mentioned only qualitatively in descriptive commentary and are never systematically identified or operationalized as analytical confounders in the study design.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2, PDF pp. 2-3; Section 3.1, PDF p. 4; Section 4, PDF pp. 6-7

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No design or analytical strategies to address confounding (such as multivariable regression, stratification by SDE network availability, or adjustment for household size and tenure) are stated or implemented. Analysis is restricted to univariate proportions and visual comparison of thematic GIS maps.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1, PDF p. 3; Section 3, PDF pp. 4-6

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Water outcomes suffer from differential measurement and unvalidated spatial extrapolation: daily water volume per person (WAI) was recorded from bi-monthly utility invoices for paying households but estimated from container and storage-tank capacities for non-paying households without verifying refill frequencies or household sharing; well-water safety claims lack microbiological/chemical testing; and values from a single centroid household were assigned to entire 500 m x 500 m (25-hectare) urban grid cells despite acknowledged intra-neighborhood heterogeneity.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1, PDF p. 1; Section 2, PDF pp. 2-3; Sections 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, PDF pp. 4-6

domain_ratings.justification: Statistical analysis is inappropriate in three respects: (1) the authors commit a clustering/unit-of-analysis fallacy by multiplying 120 sampled households by Senegal's national mean household size (9.8 persons) to claim n > 1000 and a <=3% margin of error for household-level variables; (2) the reported 99.19% response rate on 120 households is arithmetically inconsistent (119/120 = 99.17%); and (3) despite claiming to examine correlations and geostatistical spatial autocorrelation in SPSS/ArcGIS, no correlation coefficients, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or spatial autocorrelation/kriging error metrics are reported.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 & Section 2.1, PDF p. 3; Section 3, PDF pp. 4-6

evidence_quotes.criterion: Legal/institutional reform claim and main access finding
evidence_quotes.quote: This means that even areas that are not affected by poverty have a very low or poor access to water, which so far remains the perverse effect of the reform of the Senegalese water sector in 1995.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q1 / Q8 — Spatial grid household sample size and clustering/margin-of-error fallacy
evidence_quotes.quote: Grid elements were targeted, and in each element a household was selected, with a total of 120 households. In Senegal, the mean household dimension is 9.8 persons (Sylla, 2004). Based on that, the estimated number of persons involved in the survey is more than 1000, ensuring a good margin of error, no bigger than 3% (Lohr, 1999).

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q1 — Centroid GPS point selection within 500 m grid elements
evidence_quotes.quote: First, in every grid element a point was located at the centroid (center of the cell) and second, the GPS coordinates were established (Fig. 3).

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q2 / Attrition — Household survey sample size and reported response rate
evidence_quotes.quote: The survey data cover 120 households, with 99.19% response rate.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q3 / Q4 — Ad hoc 600 CFA franc poverty line operationalization
evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 3, Section 2.2 (Calculation of the poverty rate)
evidence_quotes.quote: Thus, in our calculations, as poverty line we retained 600 francs CFA. The population whose consumption is lower than this sum is regarded as poor.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q7 — Differential measurement of Water Access Index across paying and non-paying households
evidence_quotes.quote: the bi-monthly water invoices were consulted, and the values recorded. For the households who do not pay for water consumed, the water volume was evaluated daily, according to the capacity of the containers used to bring water from the wells or standpipes

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: High methodological concern under the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies (1 Unclear, 7 No across Q1-Q8). Toure et al. (2012) conducted a cross-sectional spatial survey of 120 households across a 500 m grid in Mbour, Senegal, mapping SDE piped network connections, well use, income/consumption poverty, water expenditure share, and a custom Water Access Index. While systematic spatial meshing and home-visit surveying achieved high reported participation, major threats to internal and construct validity pervade the study: (1) assigning a single centroid household's responses to an entire 25-hectare urban grid cell without population-density weighting or clear within-cell household selection criteria; (2) conflating household consumption and income while applying an ad hoc 600 CFA franc poverty threshold without reporting survey instrument details; (3) measuring daily water availability differentially (utility bills for paying households vs container/tank capacities for non-paying households) and miscalibrating domestic Water Access Index cutoffs against national total per-capita water withdrawals (0.58 m3/person/day = 580 L/day, classifying up to 250 L/person/day as 'very low access'); (4) erroneously treating 120 households multiplied by a 9.8 national average household size as >1000 independent observations to claim a <=3% margin of error; and (5) inferring water-poverty relationships and 'perverse effects' of the 1995 water sector reform purely from visual map comparisons without statistical tests of association, spatial autocorrelation metrics, or confounding control.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Cross-sectional spatial household survey (probabilistic 500 m grid sampling of 120 households integrated with GIS thematic mapping and descriptive statistics)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 1 Introduction (PDF pp. 1-2); Section 2 Materials and methods, Section 2.1 Data processing, and Section 2.2 Calculation of the poverty rate (PDF pp. 2-3); Section 3 Results and discussion, Subsections 3.1-3.4 and Figs. 6-11 (PDF pp. 4-6); Section 4 Conclusions and Acknowledgments (PDF pp. 6-7).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The primary empirical design is a single-wave quantitative cross-sectional survey of 120 households sampled on a 500 m spatial grid in Mbour to examine spatial and descriptive associations between poverty and water access/affordability, without a longitudinal cohort or quasi-experimental intervention comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I and JBI Cohort). Although Section 2.1 briefly notes in one sentence that interviews were conducted with officials from four water/municipal agencies, no qualitative methodology, coding, thematic analysis, or mixed-methods integration is presented, ruling out MMAT and CASP per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
